newsitem.title: UK: JAGGER: man of wealth, taste -- and desires.
newsitem.headline: JAGGER: man of wealth, taste -- and desires.

text.p: Mick Jagger, pouting idol of the Sixties and still a naughty boy in his fifties, turned the Rolling Stones from a bunch of scruffy young rebels into the world's most enduring rock band.

At 53, Jagger is older than President Bill Clinton, but his swagger and unique voice still fills stadiums with middle-aged fans high on nostalgia -- many accompanied by their 20-year-old offspring who go along for the classic rock 'n' roll.

If media reports are to be believed, the singer also attracts young women like moths to a guttering flame. His alleged wanderings off the marital path have prompted wife Jerry Hall to consult a divorce lawyer, newspapers said on Wednesday.
Texan fashion model Hall, with whom he had two daughters and a son, became his second wife in 1990. Jagger's daughter from his first marriage, Jade, made him a grandfather in 1992.
Jagger's good looks, wrapped around extravagant lips, and the Stones' image as rock's "Satanic Majesties," shocked British parents and delighted their children 30 years ago.
Jagger said the group were persecuted and abused. "People thought we never washed and we had fleas."

Songs like "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction" left no doubt what Jagger's main interest was outside the recording studio. His wild lifestyle, string of glamorous girlfriends and clashes with authority made him a hero to millions.

But Jagger, who dabbled in magic, bisexuality and androgyny, is now one of Britain's richest men. With houses in Manhattan, Mustique, London and France, he is -- to quote a Jagger lyric -- "a man of wealth and taste".
"They want you to be like you were in 1969," Jagger once said. "They want you to, because otherwise their youth goes with you. It's very selfish but it's understandable."
Born Michael Philip Jagger in Dartford, southeast of London, on July 26, 1943, the son of a school games teacher and a hairdresser, Jagger grew up in suburban England.
He won a place at the prestigious London School of Economics (LSE) but admitted he never took his studies seriously.
At London's Ealing Blues Club, Jagger met Brian Jones, who was recruiting for a band he called the Rollin' Stones -- the "g" was to be restored later -- after a Muddy Waters song.
In 1964 Jagger was catapulted to fame amid outrage about his surliness and the length of the group's hair.
There were riots when the band went to America and Satisfaction gave them their first U.S. and British hit.
A stream of hits followed from the misogyny in "Under My Thumb," to the anarchic "19th Nervous Breakdown" and doom-laden "Paint It Black."
Most of the Stones hits were written by Jagger and guitarist Keith Richards, a man for whom the word restraint had no meaning.
"Bourbon in hand, switchblade in his boot, guitar across his back, the law at his heels," is how singer Marianne Faithfull, one-time girlfriend of Jagger, described Richards.

In February 1967, Jagger and Richards were arrested for possession of drugs in a celebrated police bust. Jagger wore a green velvet suit and pink shirt to the trial and was sentenced to three months in jail.

He was in jail three nights before being released on bail. Many Britons believed the pair had been persecuted. The Times editor borrowed from writer Alexander Pope to plead: "Who Breaks A Butterfly on a Wheel?" Sentences were quashed on appeal.
In 1970 Jagger made a foray into the movie world, appearing in "Ned Kelly" and cult movie "Performance" which was followed by the albums "Get Yer Ya-Ya's Out" and "Sticky Fingers".

He married Nicaraguan beauty Bianca Perez Macias in 1971 and they divorced after nine tempestuous years. By the late 1970s, the Stones were being overshadowed by the punk revolution. Many fans believe "Start Me Up" off the album Tattoo You in 1981 was the Stones' last great song.
Jagger reached number one in Britain for the last time in 1985, singing "Dancing in the Street" with David Bowie and issued two solo albums "She's The Boss" (1985) and "Primitive Cool" (1987).
Many critics wrote the Stones' obituary as their albums failed to make an impact, but the band refused to lie down, taking to the stage to make a renewed impact.
The "Steel Wheels" tour in 1989 catapulted the band into the record books, earning more than $300 million. This was followed by the equally successful "Voodoo Lounge" tour.
